description: A spanned dataset, RECFM VBS: twenty-byte records in a file whose largest segment is sixteen bytes, so no segment carries more than twelve bytes of a record and neither record arrives in one piece. The first record is laid into two segments, twelve bytes and then eight, which is as few as the largest segment allows. How a writer distributes a record's bytes among that number of segments is not something any specification here decides, so what the entry holds a writer to is the count. The second is laid into three, eight and eight and four, which is a well-formed file that no correct writer would have produced, because a writer emits each record in as few segments as the largest allows and two would do, so writing these records back gives a file whose bytes are not this one's while its values are the same. All three boundaries fall inside an item rather than between two -- at twelve inside S-TEXT in the first record, and at eight inside S-TEXT and sixteen inside S-COUNT in the second -- so a consumer that decoded a segment instead of reassembling the record first fails on them. The largest segment is counted the way the segment descriptor word's own length field counts, the word included, so sixteen is four bytes of descriptor and twelve of data. Nothing in this repository's specifications states which of the two readings applies, and the entry is arranged so that it does not decide: a writer budgeting sixteen bytes of data instead lays each record into two segments as well, and writes the same fifty-six bytes.
source: docs/ir/SPEC.md, "Four framings, and none of them is a RECFM", "Where framing is consumed, and where it is emitted" and "Lengths the file node does not carry"; docs/layout/SPEC.md, "Physical framing" and "lrecl and blksize describe the dataset, not the stream"; the segment descriptor word is DFSMS's, cited in docs/ir/SPEC.md's "Governing sources" and not restated there; docs/conformance/SPEC.md, "Why the writing direction is checked by reading, and not by comparing bytes"
